opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a great question, because people sometimes assume "data-driven" means we've thrown physics out the window, and it's really the opposite.

When we trained models like FourCastNet, the main dataset was ERA5 reanalysis. Reanalysis isn't raw observations. It's decades of observations from satellites, weather balloons, ground stations, and aircraft, fused with a numerical weather model through data assimilation. So the physics is already baked in. You get a consistent, gridded picture of the atmosphere over the whole globe going back decades, and that representation respects the dynamics the simulation imposes. Raw observations are sparse and noisy. Over the oceans or in the upper atmosphere you might have very little direct measurement, and the physics model is what fills in those gaps in a physically plausible way.

That helps the model in a few ways. First, coverage and consistency. A neural network learning global atmospheric dynamics needs complete fields at every time step, and reanalysis gives you that. Second, the learned model inherits a lot of structure. Conservation laws, how energy moves between scales, how the jet stream behaves. It isn't strictly enforced, but it's strongly present in the data, so the network learns operators that roughly track the true dynamics. Third, scale. Traditional solvers are expensive, but once you've paid that cost to produce the data, you can train a model that runs tens of thousands of times faster at inference. That speed lets you run huge ensembles, thousands of members instead of fifty, which matters for extreme events and probabilistic forecasting.

There is a catch, and I want to be honest about it. If you only train on simulation output, you inherit the simulator's biases. Where the numerical model is wrong, for example with sub-grid processes like clouds and convection, the learned model will happily learn those errors too. So the direction we're excited about is combining both. Use physics-based data to learn the bulk of the dynamics, then fine-tune or correct with real observations. And use architectures like neural operators that work in function space, so they generalize across resolutions and you can bring in higher-fidelity data where you have it.

Physics-informed losses help too. You can add constraints from the governing PDEs directly into training, so even where data is limited the model is pushed toward physically consistent solutions. That makes it a lot more trustworthy when it extrapolates.

So physics simulations give us a rich, complete, structured foundation. The opportunity for AI is to go beyond them by learning faster surrogates, correcting their errors with observations, and eventually capturing processes the simulators can't resolve.

r001.rationale: It says physics is already baked into the reanalysis data and that the network learns structure from it, including atmospheric dynamics and conservation patterns.

r002.rationale: It links faster inference and larger ensembles to extreme-event forecasting, but does not say that physics information learned from the simulated data explains strong performance on extreme weather events.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the key thing to understand is that we don't actually have "raw" observations of the atmosphere in any clean sense. What we have is scattered, noisy measurements from satellites, weather stations, balloons, buoys, and the way the community turns that into something usable is through data assimilation, where you take a physics-based model and nudge it toward the observations. The product of that is a reanalysis dataset like ERA5, which is a gridded, globally consistent picture of the atmosphere going back decades.

So when we train FourCastNet, we're training on that reanalysis. And that matters for a few reasons. First, it's physically consistent. The fields obey conservation laws, the winds and pressures and temperatures relate to each other in the way the governing equations say they should, because a numerical model enforced that. The neural network doesn't have to discover those constraints from scratch out of sparse, inconsistent data. It's learning from a very well-behaved teacher.

Second, it's complete. Every grid point, every time step, every variable. That's exactly the kind of dense supervision that lets a model like a Fourier neural operator learn the mapping from the state of the atmosphere now to the state six hours from now. We're essentially learning the solution operator of the underlying PDEs, and the simulations give us samples of that operator everywhere, not just where someone happened to put a sensor.

Now, the honest caveat is that the model inherits the biases of the physics simulation. If the reanalysis is systematically wrong about, say, tropical convection or something near the surface, our model will be too. So I don't think of it as replacing physics, I think of it as distilling it. We're taking decades of expensive numerical computation and compressing it into something that runs tens of thousands of times faster, which lets us do things the traditional models can't afford, like generating huge ensembles for probabilistic forecasts.

And longer term, I think the interesting direction is closing that loop: using the learned model to go back and assimilate observations directly, or fine-tuning on real observations so you correct the simulation's biases rather than just absorbing them. But as a starting point, training on physics-prepared data is what made it possible to get skill comparable to the operational models in the first place.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the reanalysis fields are physically consistent because a numerical model enforces physical constraints, and that FourCastNet learns from this physics-based teacher.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses overall forecast skill and probabilistic ensembles but does not connect physics learned from simulations to performance on extreme weather events.

astra-6.text:
The benefit is that the model learns from data that already incorporates a lot of our understanding of physics. Weather observations are incomplete—you don’t have measurements at every point in the atmosphere. Physics-based models help combine those observations into a more complete picture of how the atmosphere evolves.

By training on that data, the AI model can learn relationships across different spatial scales and how those patterns evolve over time. Then, at inference time, it can predict that evolution much faster than running the numerical simulation itself. That opens up the possibility of running many forecasts to understand uncertainty.

But learning from physics-based data doesn’t automatically guarantee that the model obeys physical laws. You still need to evaluate its stability, its accuracy over longer forecasts, and how well it captures extreme events.

r001.rationale: It says the training data already incorporates understanding of physics and that the model learns from it.

r002.rationale: It mentions evaluating how well the model captures extreme events, but does not suggest learned physics information explains strong performance on them.

sol-6.1.text:
The key advantage is that the training data already captures a lot of the physics. We’re learning from weather data produced using numerical models that encode how the atmosphere evolves, so the neural network can learn those patterns without having to solve all of those equations explicitly at every prediction step.

That gives us an opportunity to make forecasting much faster. But learning from physically grounded data doesn’t automatically guarantee that every prediction obeys the physics. We still need to evaluate whether the model captures extreme events, whether it remains stable over longer forecasts, and where it makes mistakes. I see this as combining the strengths of physics-based simulation with the speed of machine learning.

r001.rationale: It says the data comes from numerical models that encode atmospheric physics, allowing the network to learn those patterns.

r002.rationale: It mentions evaluating how the model handles extreme events, but does not suggest that learned physics information explains strong performance on them.
